title: Lipschitz-free spaces and bounded approximation
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's construction (2026) of a countable metric space with all distances at least 1 whose Lipschitz-free space has the approximation property and not the bounded approximation property; this answers a question of Kalton. The first lesson defines the free space of a pointed metric space and the approximation properties, shows that the free space of a bounded countable space with distances at least 1 is the space l_1 with an equivalent norm, and states the theorems. The second lesson glues bounded blocks at a point and proves the main theorem from the theorem on blocks; from one named hypothesis, a theorem of Kalton on nets, it derives that the free space is not approximable by uniformly continuous maps with compact range. The third lesson constructs the blocks: regular multigraphs from random permutations whose small balls are trees, a fixed sequence of colored graphs with a colored tree limit, labels, anchors and a bounded metric. The fourth lesson turns an operator of finite rank into signed measures and studies walks that can be followed by a finite set of points. The fifth lesson builds test functions for the edges of a graph and proves by an average over all edges that no operator of finite rank and norm at most p is close to the identity at all anchors.
prerequisites: core course Functional Analysis (D20): normed spaces, the dual of a normed space and its completeness, bounded operators, compact sets; the Hahn-Banach theorem (second lesson, Section 6 only)
finite probability: uniform random permutations, independence, Chebyshev's inequality (third lesson)
the lessons prove every other fact they use, except the named hypothesis (K) of the second lesson

checks.reading: The manuscript 'A uniformly discrete counterexample to bounded approximation in Lipschitz-free spaces' (OpenAI, 26 Sep 2026, in the revision of the repository on 13 Oct 2026; six sections, one figure, about 1,440 lines of TeX) was read in full on 13 Oct 2026, and every step of its argument was derived again while the lessons were written: the coefficient estimate with the bounds 1/2 and B and the 2B-BAP; the wedge metric and its retractions; the linearization; the failure of BAP and the proof of AP for the wedge; unboundedness and the noncompact ball; the exploration of the permutation model with the collision bound, including loops and cycles of length two; the second-moment estimate; the choice of a deterministic sequence; the parameter identities; all four statements on the geometry of the block; the perturbation to a common finite support; the signed measures with the affine pairing, the total variation bound and the bump integral; the reduction of compatibility to colors; the count of walks and state sequences on the tree; the records and the two record inequalities; the consistency of the two prescriptions; the lower and upper bounds for an edge; the average over the incidences and its symmetry under reversal; the final numbers. No error found. Differences of presentation, none a correction: the linearization is obtained as the restriction of an adjoint; the frequencies are estimated by a direct bound for the mean square error without an appeal to exchangeability; the net in the nonlinear consequence is built from a dense sequence without Zorn's lemma; the average over incidences is written as a sum. Observations added in exercises, each proved: the theorem on blocks holds with 1 in place of 1/2, and with 150p^2 + 7p (the slack of the numerical argument); the states at which a bump is positive are among the states that are given up; the free space of the wedge is the l_1-sum of the free spaces of the blocks and is not isomorphic to l_1. Kalton's two papers were fetched from the archive of the author's university (free) on 13 Oct 2026; the definition of approximable spaces, the definition of a net, Theorem 4.4 and Problem 1 of the 2012 paper and Proposition 4.4 with its remarks of the 2004 paper were read; their proofs were not read. Checked by the program plan/checks_20261013/la_check.py (seven parts, exact arithmetic except one simulation: the parameter identities for p = 1 to 200; free-space norms on 14 small metric spaces by enumeration of the vertices of the Lipschitz ball, with the coefficient bounds, the linearization for all pointed 1-Lipschitz self-maps, and the wedge with the sum formula; the extension formulas; a simulation of the permutation model as an illustration; the block construction with small parameters and all four geometry statements; matched walks, records and the lemma on exceptional directions on 40 random multigraphs with random relations and on 6 blocks built on cycles, with the edge tests; the signed measures of random operators on finite spaces). All parts pass (output la_check_run_20261013.txt). In the first run the part on edge tests passed without testing anything, because in its instances every vertex was bad; the instances were replaced by blocks on cycles (143 good vertices, 326 incidences with prescriptions). No statement of the lessons was changed. The statements about the history (Kalton's question, its restatements, Dalet's theorem, the question on norms of l_1) are quoted from the manuscript and from Kalton's papers and were not checked further.

open_obligations: Named hypothesis (K): Kalton, The uniform structure of Banach spaces (2012), Theorem 4.4, the implication from (i) to (v): in a separable approximable Banach space every net that contains 0 is Lipschitz approximable. It is not proved in the programme. Only Proposition 6.2 of the second lesson (the free space of the wedge is not approximable) depends on it; the theorem on blocks, the main theorem and the corollary on norms of l_1 do not.

The completeness of the dual of a normed space, the boundedness of linear functionals in finite dimension and the Hahn-Banach theorem are taken from the core course Functional Analysis (D20); the exact locators in its text have not been looked up.

Not in the course: Kalton's theorem that the free space of every uniformly discrete space has the approximation property (the course proves it for bounded countable spaces and for the wedge); Dalet's theorem for proper spaces; any estimate of the best constants.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
